retired.note: Retired on 12 Nov 2026 as too easy; replaced by a harder version and no longer rated.

attempts.hypothesis: I believe this world has imperfect physics (motor lag/inequality, sensor bias, GPS noise) with wall mazes, narrow gaps and dead-ends, so I'm using a potential-field obstacle avoidance controller with target tracking, adaptive speed, gap-hugging heuristic, and stuck recovery.

The rover oscillated violently from conflicting potential-field forces causing extreme spin commands; I'm replacing it with gentle proportional steering (limited differential), smooth obstacle-distance speed ramping, wall-following for gaps, GPS heading correction, and calm stuck-recovery.

The attempt 3 trace shows the rover wasted ~33 seconds oscillating in place due to aggressive no-progress recovery triggering every 2.5s and a GPS heading offset that accumulated errors during the oscillation; I'm fixing this with much more conservative stuck/no-progress detection (minDist-based, hi

The trace reveals the rover wastes ~6s crawling near targets due to over-conservative distance speed caps and loses half its steering from command clipping at full throttle; I'm adding clipping compensation (scale speed to preserve steer), relaxing distance-based speed limits, and making emergency s
I believe this world rewards cautious gap finding, so I’m adding sensor-based side selection and a temporary bypass while steering toward each target.
The first run’s sharp alternating turns kept the rover spinning in place, so I’m using gentler steering with a persistent, range-guided detour when the path is blocked.
The second run hit the arena edge, so I’m adding GPS-based boundary repulsion and braking, with a persistent sensor-guided sidestep for blocked targets.
The rover’s large steering swings are causing loops at obstacles, so I’m using a smoothed, clearance-scored heading with held side detours and GPS-based edge and stuck safeguards.
I believe the clearance-scored steering made the practice run succeed, so I’m keeping it and slightly raising throttle on open paths to improve time.
The clearance and edge steering already finish reliably, so I’m making a small further throttle increase on clear paths while keeping the existing obstacle slowdowns and avoidance unchanged.
I believe the clearance-based avoidance is robust enough to use slightly more speed on open ground, so I’m raising the cruise cap while leaving the obstacle and edge safeguards unchanged.
I believe committing to a heading outside the sensor fan is an avoidable risk, so I’m keeping the proven speed and avoidance logic while scoring visible headings even when the target is behind.

I’m using a conservative local sensor reflex plus a persistent occupancy-grid A* planner, with compass/GPS correction and stuck recovery so it can learn walls and escape pockets without assuming this course.

The previous controller was unstable because it over-reacted to heading errors and avoidance while trusting noisy compass calibration; this version uses a slower, damped path follower, conservative obstacle thresholds, robust straight-line compass calibration, and simpler recovery to stay off rocks.

This keeps the proven A* occupancy planner but adds smoother longer-lookahead path following, faster arc turns in clear space, and stronger obstacle-aware speed control for better speed without giving up the prior robustness.

I’m keeping attempt 2’s proven conservative A*/sensor reflex, adding only clear-space speed boost, speed-dependent braking, and corner-safe lookahead to improve time without making tight gaps more aggressive.

I’m reverting to a slower, conservative A* planner with stronger obstacle-clearance and emergency braking, while using GPS/compass drift calibration and gentler path-following to avoid the oscillation/crash seen when speeding up.

I’m reverting to the proven conservative A*/sensor-reflex design, but replacing the unstable high-gain spin behavior with heavily damped yaw control, slower command slewing, predictive braking, and gentler recovery so it can survive gaps and still finish within the time limit.

The previous conservative planner was safe but oscillated and stalled around gaps, so I’m keeping the occupancy-grid A* but adding farther line-of-sight lookahead, lower-gain damped steering, moderate clear-space speed, and a displacement-based stall recovery to stop long spin/creep cycles.

I’m keeping attempt 7’s proven occupancy-grid A* planner with long line-of-sight lookahead, conservative sensor reflex, and displacement-based stall recovery because it finished quickly and generalises across layouts.

I assume the GPS-derived heading is more trustworthy than the compass, so this controller calibrates a compass offset from motion, steers toward the checkpoint with range-sensor repulsion, and escapes by reversing and turning when it stops making progress.

Attempt 1 mostly spun in place, flipping its pivot direction every tick, so I'm replacing it with a clearance-based steering that picks the free heading nearest the target bearing, with a sign hysteresis, a stuck-escape timer, and a slower GPS-based compass correction.

Attempts 1 and 2 never left the start pocket because they flip-flopped pivot direction and reacted to noisy short-range readings, so this version commits to turn directions, filters rays over two ticks, penalises walls and revisited cells, and escapes only after a sustained stall.

I believe the rover turns very fast and the compass is unreliable, so this version builds a 0.5 m occupancy grid from the rays, plans with A* over known-free and unknown cells, and steers gently toward a waypoint with stall-triggered reverse escapes.

The attempt-4 rover spun in place because its heading gain was too high for a very fast pivot with lag, so I'm lowering the turn gain, adding rate damping and a deadband, and keeping A* steering plus a stuck-escape that only fires after 5 s without 0.4 m of progress.

Attempt 5 finished barely inside 90 s because side repulsion flipped the wheel commands between ±0.6 and the aim point jumped between grid cells, so this version adds line-of-sight string-pulling, smoother proximity repulsion, slightly higher forward speed, and less rate damping.

Attempt 6 oscillated because its steering gain was too high for a rover that pivots at roughly 200 deg/s with lag, so I'm lowering the heading gain, dropping the rate estimate, softening the side repulsion, and loosening the speed gate that was stalling the rover.
Attempt 7 was the best run (goal at 40 s), so I'm keeping its steering, A* and escape logic nearly unchanged and only raising the speed cap slightly (0.70 to 0.75 m/s) to shorten the run.
